design: DiD across schools with staggered school-level bans (school survey on ban timing + NPD administrative data)
sample: 91 secondary schools in Birmingham, London, Leicester, Manchester; GCSE cohorts 2001-2013
headline_effect: Post-ban test scores +6.41% of a SD; gains concentrated among lowest-achieving students (~+14% SD); no effect for high achievers (published: Labour Economics 41, 61-76)

design: DiD replication of Beland & Murphy with school survey on ban timing (~75% response) + register data
sample: Swedish compulsory-school grade 9 schools, bans up to 2016
headline_effect: No impact on student performance; 'can reject even small-sized gains' (Economics of Education Review 77, 102009)

design: Synthetic control (Galicia) + DiD (Galicia, Castilla-La Mancha) vs other regions
sample: Regional bans from end-2014 (CLM) / early 2015 (Galicia); PISA 2015-2017 and official bullying case counts
ban_type: regional government bans on phones in schools
headline_effect: Galicia PISA math +10.7 and science +12.7 points by 2017 (0.6-0.8 and ~0.7-1 years of learning); CLM positive but insignificant; bullying cases per 10,000 down 15-18% (ages 12-14) and 9.5-18% (15-17), no effect under 12 (Applied Economic Analysis 30(90), 153-175)
note: Two treated regions only; PISA regional samples.

design: Event study / staggered DiD using a survey of middle schools' smartphone policies linked to administrative health, education and family registers and the national pupil survey
sample: ~400+ Norwegian middle schools (grades 8-10) adopting bans at different times up to 2018
outcomes: GP and specialist consultations for psychological symptoms; reported bullying; GPA; academic high-school track
headline_effect: Girls: fewer GP visits for psychological symptoms (about -0.2 to -0.3 visits, a sizeable share of the mean) and ~60% fewer specialist mental-health visits; bullying down for both genders (girls exposed 3 years ~-46%); girls' GPA +0.08 SD and higher academic-track enrolment; effects larger for low-SES girls; no effects for boys (NHH DP 01/2024; forthcoming Journal of Human Resources per Allcott et al. 2026)
note: Magnitudes taken from the abstract and press summaries (Boston Globe, Marginal Revolution); the PDF could not be downloaded (NHH/SSRN hosts unreachable), so verify against the paper before citing numbers.

authors: Goodyear, Randhawa, Adab, et al. (SMART Schools)
design: Cross-sectional comparison of schools with restrictive vs permissive recreational-phone policies (not causal)
sample: 30 secondary schools (20 restrictive, 10 permissive); 1,227 pupils aged 12-15
ban_type: school policy prohibiting recreational phone use during the school day
outcomes: WEMWBS mental wellbeing; anxiety; depression; sleep; attainment; phone/social-media time
headline_effect: No difference in wellbeing: adjusted mean WEMWBS difference -0.48 (95% CI -2.05 to 1.06, p=0.62); no differences in anxiety, depression, sleep, attainment or total daily phone/social-media use; less use during school hours only (Lancet Regional Health - Europe 51, 101211)

design: DiD comparing schools with high vs low pre-ban student phone activity (Advan building-level GPS) before/after the 2023 statewide ban, within one district
sample: One anonymous large urban county district (top-10 nationally); student-level records 2021-22 to 2024-25
ban_type: statewide law (HB 379) enforced as district 'no-show' rule (phones silenced and out of sight all day)
outcomes: test scores (3x/year), disciplinary incidents, suspensions, absences
headline_effect: Year 1: incidents/suspensions +~25% raw, DiD +12% suspensions, in-school suspensions +~30% for Black male students, fading by year 2; year-2 test scores +0.6 percentiles overall, +1.1 percentiles on spring test (1.3 in middle/high, 1.4 for boys); unexcused absences significantly reduced in both years (NBER WP 34388)

authors: Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow & Jacob
design: Staggered DiD (Callaway-Sant'Anna) of Yondr lockable-pouch adoption using pouch sales records, teacher survey, GPS pings, state test scores and administrative data; pre-registered
outcomes: phone use; test scores; attendance; discipline; student well-being; classroom attention; perceived online bullying
headline_effect: Phone use sharply down (teacher-reported personal use in class 61% -> 13%); test scores ~0 on average (rules out >0.007 student SD), high-school math +0.024 SD, middle school slightly negative; suspensions +~11% in year 1 then fade; subjective well-being -0.2 SD at adoption recovering to +0.16 SD by year 2; no effect on attendance, attention or online bullying (NBER WP 35132)

design: DiD contrasting middle schools without strict pre-existing rules (treated) vs schools already strict (control) around the Aug 2023 municipal ban (school-wide from Feb 2024); principal survey + admin data
ban_type: district-wide ban on non-pedagogical phone use
outcomes: standardized test scores; in-school phone use
headline_effect: Test scores +0.06 SD in treated relative to control schools; in-school phone use fell substantially

authors: Kohnstamm Instituut & Oberon (for Dutch Ministry OCW)
design: Descriptive monitoring: school-leader surveys and group interviews; no comparison group
sample: Secondary (VO), primary (BO) and special education schools (317 secondary and 313 primary leaders per press coverage); 12 focus groups
ban_type: national agreement: no phones in class from Jan 2024 (secondary) / 2024-25 (primary)
outcomes: leader-reported concentration, social climate, learning, well-being, enforcement
headline_effect: Secondary: 75% report better concentration, 59% better social climate, 28% better learning; share seeing non-educational phone use as a problem 62% -> 29%; some teachers report more physical bullying/disruption and enforcement workload. Primary: mostly no effect; 23% see better well-being/climate
note: Summary PDF from tweedekamer.nl saved locally.

authors: OECD, PISA 2022 Results Volume II (ch. 5) and 'Managing screen time' (2024)
design: Cross-sectional associations using PISA 2022 student/school questionnaires
ban_type: school reports that cell phone use on premises is not allowed
outcomes: self-reported distraction by digital devices; in-school phone use; notification habits; performance
headline_effect: About one in three OECD students attend schools banning phones; students in ban schools less likely to report distraction, but 29-30% of them still use a phone several times a day (+21% every day/almost) so bans are often unenforced; in 9 systems bans are concentrated in lower-performing schools; in some systems banned students are less likely to turn off notifications at night. No causal claim.

design: Rapid review + meta-analysis of 5 quantitative studies
headline_effect: Pooled d = 0.162 (p<0.05); larger for social well-being than for achievement (Education Sciences 14(8), 906)

outcomes: academic outcomes; mental health and wellbeing; cyberbullying
headline_effect: Mixed: 4 studies report achievement gains (2 restricted to low-achieving/low-SES samples); as many null or negative; no consistent effect on mental health or cyberbullying (J. Psychologists and Counsellors in Schools)
